_comment: Every validation result FieldShift will display, in one place, so the interface
cannot drift from what was actually measured. Each entry names the dataset it
was checked against and the script that reproduces it.
STANDING RULE, adopted after a retraction: a validation target must be a dataset
we fetched or a citation we can point at - never a remembered number. An earlier
claim of a '+18% ET0 bias' came from a remembered climatology figure; gridMET,
once actually fetched, showed -3.2%. The claim was withdrawn. Nothing goes in
this file without a reproducing command.

1.name: Validated
1.summary: Checked against independent observations at field and county scale.

2.name: Transferred
2.summary: Same engine, global-only inputs, no local observations to check against.

checks.title: Reference evapotranspiration against gridMET
checks.question: Is our FAO-56 reference ET right?
checks.result: -3.2% mean bias, r = 0.966 on daily values over 40 years
checks.detail: gridMET is an independent published product at 4 km. Our ET0 is computed from NASA POWER at 52 km with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith. A 3.2% bias at that resolution gap is better than we expected.

checks.title: Modelled water stress against observed yield
checks.question: When the model says the crop was stressed, did the yield actually fall?
checks.result: 11 of 11 correlations positive, 8 of 11 significant at p<0.05, mean r = +0.447
checks.detail: Four counties across three states, spanning soils from 84 to 212 mm/m of available water. Detrended to remove the genetic and agronomic yield trend, so what remains is year-to-year weather. Every single correlation came out with the right sign.

checks.title: Dryland versus irrigated corn penalty
checks.question: Does the model get the size of the irrigation benefit right?
checks.against: USDA NASS, irrigated and non-irrigated corn reported separately
checks.result: mean absolute error 6.0% on the yield penalty
checks.detail: A harder test than correlation, because it checks the magnitude rather than the direction. NASS reports both practices for the same county and year, which gives a direct observed penalty to compare against.

checks.title: The rotation effect itself
checks.question: Does the model get the benefit of wheat-fallow over continuous wheat right?
checks.against: USDA NASS county yields, fallow versus continuous wheat
checks.result: observed +10.8%, modelled +18.0% - we over-predict by 7 points
checks.detail: This is the check that matters most, because the rotation effect is what the tool exists to estimate, and it is the one we do not fully pass. The sensitivity sweep then showed the fallow advantage ranges +14.7% to +23.5% across 18 parameter perturbations and never reaches +10.8%, so the over-prediction is structural rather than a mis-set parameter. Most likely the model credits fallow with water it banks but does not charge it for the weeds that use some of that water. We did not add a weed parameter to close the gap, because tuning an unvalidated parameter until the answer matched would have destroyed the meaning of the agreement.

checks.title: Does the ranking survive being wrong?
checks.question: If our parameters are off, does the recommendation change?
checks.against: 18 systematic perturbations of soil water, crop coefficients, Ky and policy
checks.result: 18 of 18 perturbations leave the leading recommendation in place
checks.detail: A recommendation that flips when one parameter moves is an artefact of that parameter. This sweeps each major input across a plausible range and checks whether the top choice holds. The live sensitivity readout in the interface does the same thing for the farmer's own priority weights.

checks.title: Does the model find the bad years on its own?
checks.question: Does the model independently identify the known drought years?
checks.against: USDA NASS non-irrigated county yields, detrended, Finney County wheat and Hale County sorghum
checks.result: weak but better than chance: 4 of 12 worst-year picks agree with the harvest record against 2.6 expected by chance; correlations +0.04 and +0.19
checks.detail: This claim was previously recorded as a clean pass, naming 2012, 2011, 2002, 1988 and 2022 as drought years the model recovered unprompted. That was wrong twice over and the correction matters more than the result. First, the 'reproduce' command pointed at a script that does not produce this output - nothing did, so the claim had never actually been run. Second, the comparison was against which years a person remembers as droughts, which is exactly the inadmissible kind of target this project withdrew an earlier claim over. It is now reproduced properly against a dataset: rank the years by modelled water stress, rank them by how far the non-irrigated county harvest fell below its own trend, and compare. The model picks 4 of the 12 genuinely worst harvest years against 2.6 expected from chance - real signal, but weak, and nothing like the clean recall previously claimed. A first run that included irrigated acres gave a NEGATIVE correlation at the pilot field, which says nothing about the model and everything about comparing a rainfall-driven stress estimate against a harvest deliberately insulated from rainfall. Part of the weakness is inherent: a harvest falls for hail, freeze, disease and abandonment as well as for drought, and this model represents none of those.

checks.title: Water and carbon conservation
checks.question: Does the bookkeeping close?
checks.result: water balance closes to 1e-13 mm; a residual is treated as a bug, not a tolerance
checks.detail: Every water balance computes its own closure residual and reports it. This caught a real error in the paddy model: the pond was debited for crop water use it could not supply, because the saturated profile was an untracked store that always had water.

checks.title: Punjab water demand against the aquifer
checks.question: Is the model's irrigation demand reconcilable with the observed water table?
checks.against: CGWB observation wells via India-WRIS, 20 manual wells in Sangrur district, records up to 27 years
checks.result: direction confirmed by 20 of 20 wells (table falling 1.167 m/yr); magnitude unreconciled by 5-13x
checks.detail: The US method - correlating modelled water stress against detrended yield - cannot work here, and for a physical reason rather than a practical one. Punjab rice is continuously submerged and wheat is irrigated on demand, so the model says every year is unstressed: over 39 seasons the relative transpiration of ponded rice has a standard deviation of exactly zero and irrigated wheat 0.0008. Correlating that against yield would be correlating a constant, and district yield statistics would not have changed it. But the weather has moved from yield into water demand, where modelled rice irrigation ranges 895 to 2,338 mm, and a closed aquifer records that. Every one of the 20 wells shows a falling table, median 1.167 m/yr, IQR 0.397. The sign agrees. The magnitude does not: modelled net draft is 957-1,197 mm/yr against an observed 93-187 mm/yr across the whole plausible range of specific yield and return flow. The gap is almost certainly canal supply (our model has no canal and assumes every millimetre is pumped), lateral inflow across the district boundary, and possibly a high rice ET we have no independent product to check. What survives is the comparison between rotations, where a systematic bias largely cancels; what does not survive is any absolute claim about the aquifer's remaining life.

checks.title: Punjab yields are still unvalidated
checks.question: Has any Punjab yield been checked against observation?
checks.against: nothing - no district yield series was obtained
checks.result: not validated; the tier-2 confidence cap stands
checks.detail: Finding groundwater data did not validate the yields. The engine's yield path in Punjab rests on FAO-33 Ky values, regional recommended nitrogen rates and sowing dates entered as district practice in round numbers, none of which has been checked against a Punjab observation. The Punjab region therefore still declares a low-confidence source and no card there can read above LOW. A data trap found along the way is worth recording: India-WRIS reports manual well depths as POSITIVE metres below ground and telemetric depths as NEGATIVE. Combining them unnormalised does not produce a noisy trend, it produces a meaningless one, because half the stations would appear to move opposite to the other half for identical physical behaviour.

checks.title: Ground cover against MODIS NDVI
checks.question: When the model says the field is green, is it actually green?
checks.against: MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI, 16-day 250 m, 2003-2024, via NASA AppEEARS
checks.result: 1 of 5 pixels is a valid comparison, and it passes: Sangrur r = +0.772; the other 4 are not growing what we modelled
checks.detail: bare_ground is one of six measures a rotation is ranked on and was the only one nothing else could check, because a yield statistic says nothing about when the soil was covered. A satellite can. The check splits, and not where we expected. Sangrur's monthly NDVI profile is unmistakably rice-wheat - wheat through January to March, bare April to June between wheat harvest and rice transplanting, rice July to September - and our simulated canopy tracks it at r = +0.772 with peak greenness within about a month. That is the FIRST crop-side validation of the Punjab tier; the groundwater check tested the water, this tests the cropping. The four US pixels fail two different ways and both are our fault rather than the satellite's: Sedgwick and Holt never bare off (annual minimum NDVI 0.315 and 0.266) so they are permanent grass, not an arable rotation - Holt sits in the Nebraska Sandhills, which is cattle range; Finney and Hale do bare off but peak in late July, which is a summer crop, while we modelled winter wheat that peaks in May. The weak US correlations are therefore not evidence the canopy model is wrong, they are evidence we compared it against the wrong ground.

checks.title: The paddy water balance against observed irrigation
checks.question: Does the flooded-rice model ask for the right amount of water?
checks.against: USDA NASS irrigation census, water applied to gravity-irrigated rice in Arkansas (2013, 2018, 2023)
checks.result: still FAILS after the flood window was fixed: 981 mm modelled against 610-640 mm observed, +53%. The residual is traced to crop water use.
checks.detail: The paddy model drives the entire Punjab result and nothing had ever checked it, because India gave us no water record we could obtain. Arkansas floods its rice the same way and NASS publishes the water applied: 610-640 mm. The model asked for 1,135 mm, +77%. Percolation could not rescue it - swept 1 to 6 mm/day the closest approach was still 50% over - so the error was structural. The first suspect was the flood window: this model flooded from establishment for all 140 days, where Delta rice is drilled dry and flooded only at about the four-leaf stage, roughly 95 days. So the season model was rebuilt to run one crop through two regimes, dry then ponded then drained, with the mass balance closing to 1e-12 across both transitions. That rebuild found three further bugs on its own: the water released at the drain was counted as runoff AND as a release, the storage datum moved with the root zone so a profile that gained nothing appeared to gain, and the water filling newly explored saturated soil was never charged. Correcting the flood window was necessary and insufficient - the model still asks +53% too much. The residual is in crop water use: modelled ETc is 786 mm from a season ET0 of 680 mm and a mean coefficient of 1.13, and those FAO-56 Table 12 paddy values already include evaporation from standing water. Applying them to a crop that spends five weeks on dry soil charges open-water evaporation to a dry seedbed. There is no published basal coefficient for drill-seeded rice before the flood, which is why this has not been corrected: it is a literature question, not a coding one. Nothing was tuned - percolation, efficiency and the coefficients would each reproduce 610 mm with a plausible-looking number and each would destroy the meaning of the agreement. Punjab's rice is transplanted into an already flooded field, so Table 12 is the right table there and the dry-phase error does not apply; what carries over is that the same coefficients give 808 mm at Sangrur and nothing has checked that.

bugs_found.title: Single crop coefficients used as basal ones
bugs_found.effect: double-counted soil evaporation across every crop
bugs_found.how: FAO-56 Table 12 Kc was read where Table 17 Kcb was needed. Fixed by adding a separate kcb block, a load-time guard that kcb cannot exceed kc, and a test asserting the dual-Kc balance never reads crop.kc.

bugs_found.title: Irrigation triggered on the instantaneous root zone
bugs_found.effect: irrigated a bare seedbed from day three in all 40 seasons
bugs_found.how: Three days after sowing, roots occupy ~15 cm holding ~20 mm, so any sensible depletion threshold is crossed immediately. Real irrigators schedule against the design root zone, so scheduling now uses a management depth.

bugs_found.title: Missing FAO-56 mulch suppression
bugs_found.effect: hid roughly 700 m3/ha/yr of residue water dividend
bugs_found.how: Residue cover reduces soil evaporation by about 5% per 10% of surface covered. Without it, the mechanism by which one crop's residue saves water for the next was invisible - which is a rotation benefit the model exists to see.

bugs_found.title: RothC ignored irrigation water
bugs_found.effect: overstated soil carbon gain by about a third, in the flattering direction
bugs_found.how: The moisture term used rainfall only, so an irrigated field decomposed as if it were dry. Irrigation now enters the moisture deficit calculation.

bugs_found.title: gridMET packed integers left unscaled
bugs_found.how: The NetCDF scale_factor of 0.1 was not applied. A plausibility guard now rejects physically impossible values rather than passing them through.

bugs_found.title: DEM slope noise inflated erosion 17-fold
bugs_found.effect: 5.77% slope where the true value is 0.25%
bugs_found.how: On near-flat ground the vertical noise in a 30 m DEM is comparable to the real gradient, so a 3x3 Horn gradient measures noise. Slope is now a least-squares planar fit over about 300 m, verified to preserve genuine slopes.

bugs_found.title: Williams erosion K factor unit error
bugs_found.how: 0.3526 against a published range of 0.03-0.045. The US-to-SI conversion factor of 0.1317 was missing, and a range guard now catches it.

bugs_found.title: Nitrogen rationed monthly instead of seasonally
bugs_found.how: 11 kg of nitrogen supplied against 117 demanded, because a crop was only allowed the current month's mineralisation. Nitrogen is now balanced over the season.

bugs_found.title: Production summed across crops of different water content
bugs_found.effect: made a maize-potato rotation look 2.5x more productive than rice-wheat
bugs_found.how: Found when the Punjab region introduced potato. 25 t/ha of fresh tubers against 4 t/ha of grain is a six-fold difference in sale weight but only about 1.5-fold in dry matter. The production objective now sums dry matter. On the US sites every crop was grain, so this was latent.

bugs_found.title: Puddling water spilled the bund on day one
bugs_found.effect: 80 mm of a 180 mm paddy establishment application booked as runoff
bugs_found.how: Found by a test. Puddling water wets and saturates the profile before anything stands on the surface; it was being routed straight into the pond.

bugs_found.title: Groundwater depth sign flips between acquisition modes
bugs_found.effect: would have produced a meaningless district trend, not merely a noisy one
bugs_found.how: India-WRIS reports CGWB manual well depths as positive metres below ground and telemetric piezometer depths as negative. A naive combination has half the stations appearing to rise while the other half fall, for identical physical behaviour. Depth is now normalised per acquisition mode explicitly rather than with abs(), which would also have silently swallowed genuinely artesian readings instead of rejecting them.

bugs_found.title: A year-long groundwater query silently returned only telemetric data
bugs_found.effect: every long-record manual well was crowded out of the result
bugs_found.how: The endpoint caps a response at 50,000 rows and the telemetric piezometers report every few minutes, so a single 1994-2024 request came back entirely full of GPRS readings from 20 stations with zero manual wells. The adapter now fetches year by year, falls back to month by month when a year still hits the cap, and refuses rather than accepting a response at the page limit.

bugs_found.title: Site coordinates were county reference points, not verified cropland
bugs_found.effect: 4 of 5 validation pixels were not growing the rotation being validated against them
bugs_found.how: We placed each field at a county reference coordinate and assumed the 250 m cell beneath it was arable land growing the modelled rotation. MODIS says otherwise: two sites never bare off at all and are permanent grass, and two bare off but green up in high summer rather than spring, so they grow a summer crop and not the winter wheat-fallow we simulated. Caught only because we went looking for an independent check on ground cover. The fix is to move the sample points onto verified cropland using a land-cover product; until then the US arm of the NDVI check is reported as inconclusive rather than quietly averaged in.

bugs_found.title: The paddy model floods for the whole season, not the flood window
bugs_found.effect: over-predicts rice irrigation by roughly 50% where the two differ
bugs_found.how: Found by the first independent test the paddy model has ever had. Drill-seeded rice is dry for about five weeks before the permanent flood goes on, so holding water from establishment pays evaporation and percolation on 45 days that are never flooded. Quantified rather than fixed: a correct fix means splitting one rice crop into a dry phase and a ponded phase, and making that change against a target we already know would be fitting rather than modelling.

bugs_found.title: The drain released water was counted twice
bugs_found.effect: mass balance off by ~400 mm on any season with a drain
bugs_found.how: Water let off at the drain was added to the runoff series before infiltration was computed, so infiltration went negative by the whole pond depth, and the release was then subtracted again on the storage side. Invisible until a crop existed that is flooded for only part of its season.

bugs_found.title: The water balance datum moved with the root zone
bugs_found.effect: a profile that gained nothing appeared to gain 51 mm
bugs_found.how: Storage was measured against field capacity, which rises as roots deepen - so under a flood, where depletion is pinned at zero, growing roots silently created water. Storage is now measured against the wilting point of the current root zone, the same datum either side of a flood-up or a drain.

bugs_found.title: Root growth was credited on days the regime changed
bugs_found.effect: leaked exactly one day's root growth at every drain
bugs_found.how: The root-growth bookkeeping ran before the flood-up and drain handlers, both of which reset the depletion - so the credit was kept and the matching depletion thrown away. The bookkeeping now runs after the transitions.

bugs_found.title: A validation claim that had never been run
bugs_found.effect: an unsupported 'pass' displayed in the interface for days
bugs_found.how: The drought-recall check named specific years and pointed at a reproduce command that does not produce them. Nothing in the repository did. It was caught only when someone asked where the claim was backed up. Writing the script that reproduces it downgraded the check from pass to partial. Every other entry has since been re-checked against its own command.
